## Verdict

missing

## Bearer

ConnectivityPermissionSystemImpl.requestPermission — core-platform/src/main/kotlin/com/mgilli/core/platform/connectivity/permission/ConnectivityPermissionSystemImpl.kt:54-59
SensorPermissionSystemImpl.requestPermission — app-wear/src/main/java/com/mgilli/app_wear/sensor/permission/SensorPermissionSystemImpl.kt:84-91

Same pattern in both, applied independently: neither depends on the other, and the fix is identical in shape at each site.

## Trigger

The activity being destroyed by the OS while the system permission dialog is on screen, before `onPermissionResult` is called back — nothing observes it

## Today

Both `requestPermission()` implementations create a `CompletableDeferred<Boolean>`, launch the system dialog (`launcher.launch()` directly in `ConnectivityPermissionSystemImpl`, through `lifecycle.withResumed { launcher.launch(...) }` in `SensorPermissionSystemImpl`), then `return deferred.await()` with no timeout. The only thing that ever completes `pendingResult` is `onPermissionResult(granted: Boolean)`, called from the launcher's own callback. If the hosting activity is destroyed before that callback arrives, `onPermissionResult` is never invoked, `pendingResult` is never completed, and the suspended coroutine never resumes for the remaining life of the process.

Both call sites are reached at application startup, unconditionally on the app's first launch: `HomeViewModel.init` (app-wear/src/main/java/com/mgilli/app_wear/home/HomeViewModel.kt:58) calls `connectivityPermissionManager.onLaunch()`, which calls `system.requestPermission()` on first launch (core-domain/src/main/kotlin/com/mgilli/core/domain/connectivity/ConnectivityPermissionManager.kt:19); `ProfileViewModel.init` (app-phone/src/main/java/com/mgilli/hyroxtracker/ui/profile/ProfileViewModel.kt:132) calls `hrPermissionSystem.requestPermission()` directly, and the wear side's own `HomeViewModel.init:64` reaches `SensorPermissionManager.onLaunch()` (app-wear/src/main/java/com/mgilli/app_wear/sensor/permission/SensorPermissionManager.kt:23), which calls `system.requestPermission()` the same way.

Both `SensorPermissionState` (app-wear/src/main/java/com/mgilli/app_wear/sensor/permission/SensorPermissionState.kt) and `ConnectivityPermissionState` (core-domain/src/main/kotlin/com/mgilli/core/domain/connectivity/ConnectivityPermissionState.kt) are `sealed interface` with exactly two cases: `Granted` and `Fallback`. `requestPermission()` itself returns a plain `Boolean` in both implementations — there is no third value distinct from "denied" that a timeout could return today.

The one piece of the intended distinction that does already exist: `onPermissionResult`'s own KDoc states the `KEY_HAS_REQUESTED` flag "is only set here, on a real answer from the system — a dialog dismissed by the OS without ever calling back … must not consume it." That reservation covers an OS-dismissed dialog, not an activity destroyed mid-wait, and nothing today makes the wait itself return in that case at all.

## Expected

`requestPermission()` bounds its `deferred.await()` with a timeout, in both `ConnectivityPermissionSystemImpl` and `SensorPermissionSystemImpl`. On expiry, the call resolves rather than suspending indefinitely, and the outcome is treated as an unanswered dialog, never as a stated refusal — the user was not asked and answered no; the request was simply never delivered an answer. `KEY_HAS_REQUESTED` is left exactly as it stood before the call, the same way `onPermissionResult`'s KDoc already reserves for a callback-less OS dismissal, so `canShowSystemPrompt()` keeps offering a further prompt rather than reading as a permanent denial.

A second gap this fix cannot avoid: `requestPermission()`'s signature returns a plain `Boolean` in both `ConnectivityPermissionSystem`/`SensorPermissionSystem` interfaces, and `SensorPermissionState`/`ConnectivityPermissionState` each carry only `Granted` and `Fallback`. Neither the interface nor either state type has room today for a third outcome distinct from "denied" and "granted." Representing "dialog unanswered" as its own outcome — as opposed to silently folding it into `false`/`Fallback` — requires a value that does not exist yet, on both the boolean-returning signature and the two-case state each system feeds into via `SensorPermissionManager.onLaunch`/`requestAgain` and `ConnectivityPermissionManager.onLaunch`/`requestAgain`.
